_comment: Surgery pathway for deep vein thrombosis. Wells score is the severity anchor; duplex non-compressibility is the confirmatory sign; provoked or unprovoked decides duration. Shared leg-vein examination skills are referenced, never redefined.
name: Deep vein thrombosis
fullName: Deep vein thrombosis: assessment with the Wells score and duplex confirmation
subtitle: Wells score
oneLine: A painful swollen leg after stillness, sorted by Wells likelihood and confirmed by duplex

skill.reasoning.deep.basics.title: What deep vein thrombosis is
skill.reasoning.deep.basics.oneLine: Clot in the deep leg veins from stasis, injury and clotting tendency, liable to travel to the lungs
skill.reasoning.deep.basics.why: A swollen leg is only dangerous because of where the clot can go next: calf thrombi propagate upward and break off to the lungs, so understanding stasis, injury and hypercoagulability as one mechanism is what turns a leg ache into an urgent assessment rather than reassurance.

teach.heading: Three forces make one clot
teach.body:
Thrombosis arises from the triad of venous stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability, usually coupled with an inflammatory trigger. Platelets release mediators that recruit neutrophils, the resulting traps drive platelet clumping and thrombin generation, and clots flourish where flow is slow, oxygen low and proinflammatory genes switched on.

Lower-limb thrombosis usually begins in the calf veins and may propagate to the popliteal, femoral and iliac veins. When thrombi detach they embolise through the vena cava and right heart to lodge in the pulmonary arteries.

rows: Idle calf muscles under anaesthesia, in bed, or on a long journey
Blood pools in the deep veins and clots
Surgery, trauma, fractures and venous catheters
Exposes a surface that triggers clotting
Cancer, pregnancy, hormonal pills, inherited deficiencies

teach.heading: Mostly silent, sometimes fatal
teach.body:
Deep vein thrombosis is mostly an asymptomatic disease, and only about one in four cases produces even minor complaints. Because of this silence, preventive care during stillness matters more than early symptoms, and a fatal embolus may be the very first indication that thrombosis was present.

The index of suspicion therefore comes from the setting rather than the story: recent surgery, delivery, plaster, long bed rest or a long journey sitting still should raise the question even when the leg complaint sounds modest.

teach.heading: What embolisation explains
points: Unexplained breathlessness is the commonest symptom when clot reaches the lungs, and signs there are nonspecific.
Failure to improve despite standard therapy for concurrent heart failure or pneumonia is a clue to coexisting embolism.
Many patients with embolism have no demonstrable leg thrombosis left, because the leg thrombus has already fully embolised.
A paradoxical embolism to the arterial circulation can occur through a patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect.

pitfalls: Treating a normal-looking leg as proof against thrombosis, when most thrombosis is silent.
Assuming the absence of leg signs excludes embolism in a breathless patient.
Forgetting the inflammatory trigger that couples stasis and injury to an actual clot.

probes.q: Where does lower-limb deep vein thrombosis usually begin, and where can it spread?
probes.a: It usually begins in the calf veins and may propagate upward to the popliteal, femoral and iliac veins.

probes.q: Why can a patient have a pulmonary embolism with no demonstrable leg thrombosis?
probes.a: Because the leg thrombus may already have fully embolised, leaving no residual clot in the leg to find.

probes.q: Name the three forces of clot formation and give one clinical example of each.
probes.a: Venous stasis such as idle calf muscles in bed, endothelial injury such as surgery or trauma, and hypercoagulability such as cancer, pregnancy or an inherited deficiency.

skill.reasoning.deep.signs.title: The thrombosis picture at the bedside
skill.reasoning.deep.signs.oneLine: Swelling around the ankle and calf, a tender calf, and the white leg versus the blue leg
skill.reasoning.deep.signs.why: The examination of suspected thrombosis is subtle and easily over-read: swelling is the one sign that matters, no provocative calf manoeuvre should be performed, and the difference between a pale swollen leg and a blue congested one is the difference between routine anticoagulation and a limb emergency.

teach.heading: Swelling is the sign that steals the show
teach.body:
Swelling of the leg is the most important physical feature, typically found around the ankle or a little higher up, with the calf muscles swollen and measurable against the other side. The extent maps the level: calf confinement suggests calf veins, while thigh involvement suggests iliac-level thrombosis.

The muscles containing the thrombosed veins feel hard as well as tender, and that change in texture matters more than tenderness alone, because many conditions make a calf tender but few make it stiff and hard.

teach.heading: Do not test the calf with provocative manoeuvres
teach.body:
Do not try to elicit calf pain by forceful dorsiflexion of the foot with the knee extended or by squeezing the relaxed calf from side to side. These historical manoeuvres, the Homans dorsiflexion sign and the Moses calf squeeze sign, are obsolete: they are insensitive and nonspecific, they distress a patient with an acutely thrombosed leg, and rough handling carries a theoretical risk of dislodging clot toward the lungs.

Suspected thrombosis is assessed by clinical likelihood with the Wells assessment, then d-dimer and/or compression duplex as the tier directs, with duplex as the confirmatory test. Record swelling, warmth, calf firmness and tenderness found on gentle inspection and palpation, feel the pulses, and defer the walking tourniquet test, leaving deep patency to duplex.

teach.heading: The hot leg and the blue leg
teach.body:
With venous outflow blocked the superficial veins dilate to carry blood home, and the limb feels hot. When one deep system blocks, the leg swells pale and very painful, the so-called white leg. When all the main veins block, the skin turns congested and blue, the so-called blue leg.

The blue congested leg with diffuse swelling is the most serious form, a limb-threatening emergency in which arterial pulses may later disappear and venous gangrene can develop. It must be recognised at a glance and escalated, not worked up routinely.

teach.heading: What is often absent
points: Most thrombosis produces no signs at all, so a near-normal leg never excludes the diagnosis.
Fever, when present, is usually slight rather than the shaking fever of cellulitis.

The surface thrombosis of an inflamed vein after infusion feels like a hard tender cord under red skin. This superficial thrombosis is a different disease, but it still carries a real risk of concurrent or subsequent deep vein thrombosis and embolism to the lungs, so the leg needs whole-leg compression duplex to exclude coexisting deep thrombosis.
Chest pain, breathlessness or haemoptysis mean embolism may already have occurred, even with modest leg signs.

pitfalls: Calling every tender calf a thrombosis without noting whether the muscle is also hard and swollen.
Performing dorsiflexion or calf squeezing to test for thrombosis: these obsolete manoeuvres add no accuracy, distress the patient, and risk dislodging clot.
Missing the blue congested whole-limb swelling that marks the limb-threatening emergency.

probes.q: What is the single most important physical sign of deep vein thrombosis?
probes.a: Swelling of the leg, typically around the ankle and calf, with the calf measurably larger than the other side.

probes.q: Why must dorsiflexion and calf squeezing not be used to test for thrombosis, and what is done instead?
probes.a: Because these historical manoeuvres are obsolete, insensitive and nonspecific, and they distress the patient with a theoretical risk of dislodging clot; likelihood is graded with the Wells assessment and testing proceeds to d-dimer and/or compression duplex.

probes.q: How do you distinguish the pale painful swollen leg from the blue congested one, and why does it matter?
probes.a: The pale white leg reflects obstruction of one deep system, while the blue leg reflects blockage of all main veins with congested skin; the blue leg is the most serious form and a limb-threatening emergency needing escalation.

skill.reasoning.deep.differential.title: What else a painful swollen leg can be
skill.reasoning.deep.differential.oneLine: Baker cyst, muscle strain and cellulitis first, then surface thrombosis, arterial ischaemia and the lung
skill.reasoning.deep.differential.why: A painful swollen calf is one of the least specific presentations in surgery, and each mimic fails in a different direction: cellulitis needs antibiotics not anticoagulation, a muscle strain needs rest not a scan, and an ischaemic leg needs revascularisation within hours, so the differential is not an academic list but the thing that stops the wrong treatment.

teach.heading: Three mimics of sudden calf pain
teach.body:
A ruptured Baker cyst announces itself with sudden severe calf discomfort, often in a patient with a known swollen knee, and ultrasound separates it from thrombosis. A calf muscle strain follows a clear injury or unaccustomed exertion, with a discrete tender spot rather than diffuse swelling.

Cellulitis is the mimic that most often causes wrong treatment: fever with chills heralds infection rather than thrombosis, the skin is hot and red with a spreading edge, and the patient looks infected. When fever and chills lead the picture, treat infection first and exclude thrombosis alongside, not instead.

teach.heading: Vein against vein
teach.body:
Superficial thrombophlebitis is an inflammatory condition, often after an intravenous infusion or in varicose veins, with pain as the main feature, inflamed skin and a hard tender cord along the vein. It was once regarded as benign, but it carries a meaningful risk of concurrent or subsequent deep vein thrombosis and embolism to the lungs, especially when extensive or near the saphenofemoral or saphenopopliteal junction.

Such legs need whole-leg compression duplex to exclude coexisting deep thrombosis, and significant-length disease needs anticoagulation.

Chronic venous insufficiency and the post-thrombotic limb swell over months with eczema, pigmentation and sometimes ulceration, not over days. Lymphoedema is typically chronic, non-pitting and painless, often with thickened skin, which is a different tempo and texture from an acute clot.

teach.heading: Artery and lung in the differential
teach.body:
Acute limb ischaemia is the cannot-miss alternative: a pale, cold, pulseless leg with severe pain needs revascularisation within hours, and the arterial pulses decide it at the bedside. Never assess a swollen leg without feeling the pulses.

Breathlessness with pleuritic pain may be embolism, pneumonia or heart failure, and these coexist as often as they compete: failure to improve with standard heart failure or pneumonia therapy is itself a clue that embolism is present as well. A swollen leg with chest symptoms needs both territories worked up, not one or the other.

pitfalls: Starting anticoagulation for cellulitis because the leg is red and swollen, without noting fever with chills.
Ordering a duplex for a clear muscle strain with an injury history, instead of examining first.
Forgetting the arterial pulses, so an ischaemic leg is worked up as a venous one until it is too late.

probes.q: A patient has sudden severe calf pain after feeling something pop behind the knee. What is the leading alternative to thrombosis?
probes.a: A ruptured Baker cyst, with sudden severe calf discomfort, separated from thrombosis by ultrasound.

probes.q: How do fever and chills help separate cellulitis from deep vein thrombosis?
probes.a: Fever with chills heralds cellulitis rather than thrombosis, in which fever is usually slight or absent.

probes.q: What single bedside step excludes the cannot-miss arterial alternative in a painful swollen leg?
probes.a: Feeling the arterial pulses: a pale cold pulseless leg is acute limb ischaemia needing revascularisation within hours, not a venous workup.

rubric.text: Separates Baker cyst, strain and cellulitis by story and fever
Distinguishes superficial thrombophlebitis and chronic venous or lymphatic swelling by tempo
Checks pulses and considers coexisting embolism, pneumonia or heart failure

skill.investigation.deep.workup.title: Confirming thrombosis and looking for embolism
skill.investigation.deep.workup.oneLine: Wells likelihood first, duplex to confirm the leg, d-dimer only to exclude at low likelihood
skill.investigation.deep.workup.why: Tests for suspected thrombosis answer two different questions, is there a clot in the leg and has any reached the lungs, and using the wrong test for the wrong question wastes the diagnosis: d-dimer cannot confirm anything, a scan should not wait for blood results in a high-likelihood leg, and chest tests are for chest symptoms, not routine screening.

teach.heading: Decide likelihood before ordering anything
teach.body:
Estimate clinical likelihood first, using the Wells assessment, which is validated in ambulatory patients but not in hospitalised ones. A low-likelihood leg can be evaluated with d-dimer alone, while a high-likelihood leg should skip d-dimer and go straight to imaging.

The PERC rule identifies the low-risk chest patient who needs no further testing: under 50, pulse under 100, saturation 95 percent or more, no prior clot, no unilateral leg swelling, no oestrogen use, no haemoptysis, and no surgery or trauma within four weeks.

teach.heading: The scan that confirms the leg
teach.body:
Compression duplex with Doppler is the first-line test for the leg. A normal vein collapses completely with gentle transducer pressure, while an acutely thrombosed vein stays distended and non-compressible, and absent flow confirms the blockage.

A negative leg scan does not exclude embolism to the lungs, because the leg thrombus may already have fully embolised. Where the leg scan is equivocal, or pelvic veins need seeing, MR venography with contrast is the next step.

teach.heading: D-dimer rules out, never rules in
teach.body:
Quantitative plasma d-dimer has sensitivity over 95 percent for embolism and is useful for exclusion at low pretest probability, with a negative result under 0.4 mcg per mL carrying a negative predictive value over 95 percent. But it is nonspecific: infarction, pneumonia, sepsis, cancer, the postoperative state and late pregnancy all raise it.

It is therefore rarely useful in hospitalised patients, in whom levels are frequently raised by systemic illness. The age-adjusted cutoff of age times 10 ng per mL in patients over 50 reduces unnecessary scans, but it applies to suspected embolism only, never to suspected acute thrombosis of the leg.

teach.heading: When the chest is involved
points: CT pulmonary angiography with contrast is the principal test for embolism, and a right-to-left ventricular diameter ratio over 1 on the scan predicts higher 30-day mortality.
Ventilation perfusion scanning is second line, reserved for patients who cannot take contrast, including renal failure and pregnancy.
The commonest ECG findings are sinus tachycardia and T-wave inversion in V1 to V4 from right heart strain; the S1Q3T3 pattern is relatively specific but insensitive.
Troponin rises with right ventricular microinfarction and natriuretic peptides with myocardial stretch, grading severity rather than confirming diagnosis.
Echocardiography cannot rule embolism out, since most patients have a normal study, but it detects mimics such as infarction, tamponade and dissection.

pitfalls: Ordering d-dimer in a high-likelihood leg and waiting for it before scanning, delaying the diagnosis that the scan would give.
Using the age-adjusted d-dimer cutoff for a suspected leg thrombosis, where it is not validated.
Treating a normal echocardiogram as excluding embolism, when most embolism patients have normal studies.

probes.q: What is the first-line imaging test for suspected leg thrombosis, and what is its diagnostic sign?
probes.a: Compression duplex ultrasonography with Doppler; loss of vein compressibility, with the thrombosed vein staying distended and non-compressible.

probes.q: A high-likelihood leg has a negative d-dimer. Can thrombosis be excluded?
probes.a: No. A high-likelihood patient should skip d-dimer and go straight to imaging; d-dimer excludes only at low pretest probability.

probes.q: Why is d-dimer rarely useful in a hospitalised patient with a swollen leg?
probes.a: Because levels are frequently raised by systemic illness such as sepsis, cancer, infarction or the postoperative state, so a positive result cannot confirm thrombosis and a negative one is uncommon.

skill.reasoning.deep.diagnosis.title: Diagnosis and likelihood: the Wells score
skill.reasoning.deep.diagnosis.oneLine: Wells sorts likely from unlikely, duplex confirms, and provoked or not decides what follows
skill.reasoning.deep.diagnosis.why: A diagnosis of swollen leg says nothing about what to do next, while a diagnosis that states the Wells likelihood, the confirmatory test and whether the clot was provoked contains the whole plan: scan or exclude, treat for three months or indefinitely, and look for embolism or not.

teach.heading: Wells sorts likely from unlikely
teach.body:
The Wells assessment estimates the clinical likelihood of thrombosis or embolism and is validated in ambulatory patients, not in hospitalised ones. Its output is two-tiered: likely or unlikely for the leg, with a low-to-moderate band for the chest.

The tier drives the test: low-likelihood leg disease can be evaluated with d-dimer alone, and a negative result excludes it, while high-likelihood disease skips d-dimer and goes straight to imaging. Scoring likelihood before testing is what keeps scans for those who need them and d-dimer for those it can actually clear.

rows: Seek another diagnosis for the swelling
High likelihood, or any positive d-dimer
Breathlessness or pleuritic pain with clot
Grade with CT angiography and markers

teach.heading: Name the clot completely
teach.body:
A complete diagnostic statement names the site and extent, proximal or calf, the likelihood tier that led to testing, the confirmatory finding, and whether the event was provoked by surgery, trauma or immobility or arose unprovoked. Provoked or not is not decoration: it decides duration.

Where embolism is confirmed, stratify it: high-risk disease with hypotension and shock, intermediate-risk disease with right ventricular dysfunction at normal pressure, and low-risk disease with an excellent outlook. A diffusely blue swollen leg is the limb emergency that sits outside this grading and needs escalation on its own.

pitfalls: Stating thrombosis without a likelihood tier, so nobody can tell whether d-dimer or direct imaging was the right test.
Applying the Wells assessment to a hospitalised patient, in whom it is not validated.
Calling a provoked postoperative clot and an unprovoked one by the same name, hiding the different durations they need.

probes.q: What two tiers does the Wells assessment give for suspected leg thrombosis, and how does each tier change testing?
probes.a: Likely or unlikely; low-likelihood disease can be evaluated with d-dimer alone, while high-likelihood disease skips d-dimer and goes straight to imaging.

probes.q: What must a complete diagnostic statement for thrombosis contain beyond the word thrombosis?
probes.a: Site and extent, the likelihood tier, the confirmatory finding, and whether the event was provoked or unprovoked, since provocation decides duration.

probes.q: How is confirmed embolism stratified, and where does the blue swollen leg sit?
probes.a: High-risk with hypotension and shock, intermediate-risk with right ventricular dysfunction at normal pressure, and low-risk with excellent outlook; the blue congested leg is a separate limb emergency needing escalation regardless of grade.

rubric.text: States the Wells tiers and links each to the correct test
Names site, proof and provoked or unprovoked status
Stratifies embolism and recognises the limb emergency

skill.treatment.deep.management.title: Managing thrombosis and preventing the next one
skill.treatment.deep.management.oneLine: Prompt anticoagulation by setting, duration by provocation, and compression with mobilisation alongside
skill.treatment.deep.management.why: The two decisions that change outcome are speed and duration: anticoagulation started promptly stops extension and embolism, while provoked or unprovoked decides three months or longer, and getting either wrong in either direction leaves a clot untreated or a patient bleeding without reason.

teach.heading: Start therapeutic anticoagulation promptly
teach.body:
Direct oral anticoagulants are first line for most patients, with apixaban and rivaroxaban needing no parenteral lead-in, while edoxaban needs five to ten days of heparin first. Weight-based low-molecular-weight heparin is preferred in cancer-associated thrombosis and in pregnancy, and is avoided when creatinine clearance is under 30 mL per minute.

Unfractionated heparin suits high bleeding risk or planned thrombolysis because it is rapidly reversible, titrated to an aPTT of 1.5 to 2.5 times control. Warfarin, overlapped with heparin for at least five days until the INR is 2 to 3 for 24 hours, remains the standard in antiphospholipid syndrome rather than a direct oral agent.

teach.heading: The unstable lung clot is a different emergency
teach.body:
Systemic thrombolysis, or catheter-directed therapy or embolectomy, is reserved for high-risk embolism with haemodynamic instability: hypotension with a large clot burden, presenting with breathlessness, faintness, falling pressure and cyanosis and capable of causing shock and death.

Where anticoagulation is contraindicated, or clots recur despite therapy, an inferior vena cava filter is considered, particularly when cardiopulmonary reserve is marginal. Supportive care runs alongside: oxygen, haemodynamic support and analgesia.

teach.heading: Duration is decided by provocation
teach.body:
A clot provoked by a transient risk factor such as surgery, trauma or immobility is treated for three months. Unprovoked disease, cancer-associated thrombosis, thrombophilia and recurrence need extended or indefinite therapy, with bleeding risk reviewed yearly.

After six to twelve months of treatment, a reduced rivaroxaban dose of 10 mg daily is a listed option for extended secondary prevention. Investigate for underlying malignancy or thrombophilia where appropriate, escalate high-risk disease to a higher centre or embolism response team, and counsel on bleeding risk and, for inherited states, the family implications.

teach.heading: Everything around the drug, in Indian practice
points: Graduated compression and early mobilisation accompany anticoagulation, and manage the blue congested leg as a limb-threatening emergency.
Prefer low-molecular-weight heparin in pregnancy and counsel against direct oral agents there.
Use affordable generic anticoagulants, including supply through government pharmacies and Jan Aushadhi outlets, and confirm duplex availability at the district hospital before referring onward.
Refer to a higher centre for thrombolysis, catheter procedures or embolectomy rather than attempting them without support.
Arrange thrombophilia and cancer screening where the clot is unprovoked, and counsel about the small long-term risks of post-thrombotic limb swelling and, after embolism, persistent breathlessness.

pitfalls: Delaying the first anticoagulant dose while waiting for exhaustive tests in a confirmed high-likelihood patient.
Prescribing a direct oral agent for antiphospholipid syndrome, where warfarin is the standard.
Stopping at three months an unprovoked or cancer-associated clot that needs extended therapy with yearly bleeding review.

probes.q: How long is a clot provoked by surgery treated, and what decides a longer course?
probes.a: Three months for a transient provoked event; unprovoked disease, cancer, thrombophilia or recurrence needs extended or indefinite therapy.

probes.q: Which anticoagulant is preferred in pregnancy and in cancer-associated thrombosis?
probes.a: Weight-based low-molecular-weight heparin, avoided when creatinine clearance is under 30 mL per minute.

probes.q: When is thrombolysis or catheter therapy indicated rather than anticoagulation alone?
probes.a: In high-risk embolism with haemodynamic instability and hypotension, with catheter therapy or embolectomy where lysis is contraindicated.

skill.particulars.demographics.expect: In suspected thrombosis the setting does the heavy work: a postoperative, postpartum, or long-travel patient carries a high pre-test probability before any symptom is weighed, and an active cancer or past clot raises it further. Record the date of the operation, delivery or journey, not just its occurrence.

chapters.title: History of presenting illness
chapters.blurb: One leg, days old, and the chest questions that must never be skipped

skill.hx.chief_complaints.expect: A typical presentation reads in days, not months: calf ache and swelling for two to four days after stillness, worse on standing and walking, eased by elevation. That tempo alone should move you away from chronic venous disease or lymphoedema.

skill.hx.deep.leg_swelling.expect: Expect unilateral pain and swelling of days duration, often starting in the calf, with bursting pain on walking. Always close with the chest screen: new breathlessness, pleuritic pain, cough or haemoptysis would mean the clot may already have travelled.

chapters.title: Past, personal, drug and family history
chapters.blurb: Stasis, cancer, hormones and past clots decide likelihood and duration

chapters.title: General examination
chapters.blurb: A leg disease with systemic clues

skill.gen.appearance.expect: Most patients look systemically well, which is exactly why the diagnosis is missed: a comfortable patient with one swollen leg still needs the full likelihood assessment. Breathlessness, tachycardia or low saturation would instead warn of embolism.

skill.gen.vitals.expect: Expect near-normal vitals in isolated leg thrombosis, sometimes with a slight fever. Tachycardia, tachypnoea or desaturation are not features of the leg clot; they are warnings that embolism must be assessed urgently.

skill.gen.edema.expect: Expect unilateral pitting oedema from the calf or ankle upward, measurably larger than the other side. Bilateral ankle oedema points elsewhere, toward cardiac, renal or drug causes rather than a single deep system.

chapters.title: Examination of the leg veins
chapters.blurb: Swelling measured, no provocative calf tests, pulses never forgotten

skill.exam.surg.varicose_inspection_palp.expect: Inspect and palpate for unilateral swelling, warmth, redness and dilated surface veins carrying blood home around the blockage. Note calf hardness and tenderness, and look for the pale massively painful leg or the blue congested leg, which changes everything.

skill.exam.surg.arterial_pulses_lower.expect: Feel every pulse before concluding anything venous: a pale, cold, pulseless leg is acute ischaemia needing revascularisation within hours, not a venous workup. Present pulses are also a required negative before compression is advised.

skill.exam.surg.perthes_deep_vein_patenc.expect: In suspected acute thrombosis, do not perform the full walking tourniquet test: forceful exercise against a blocked deep system bursts with pain and risks dislodging clot. A gentle assessment only, with the warning documented, and the definitive answer left to duplex.

stations.title: Examine the swollen leg
stations.task: This 52 year old woman is ten days after abdominal surgery and has a three-day painful swelling of the left leg. Examine her lower limbs and present your findings with your assessment of likelihood.
examinerQuestions: Her left calf is hard, tender and 3 cm larger than the right, and the leg is warm with dilated surface veins. What is your Wells likelihood, and what test comes next?
Why will you not perform the full walking tourniquet test on this leg, and what do you do instead?
Her foot pulses are absent and the leg is pale and cold. What has changed, and what is the time-critical next step?

stations.title: Take a thrombosis history and triage
stations.task: This 46 year old man has a two-day painful swelling of the right calf after a long bus journey. Take a focused history in six minutes and be ready to state his likelihood and your next test.
examinerQuestions: Which four facts in his story raise the likelihood of thrombosis, and what would lower it?
He now mentions breathlessness since this morning. How does that change your urgency and your tests?
His d-dimer returns negative but you scored him high likelihood. What do you do, and why?

cases.title: A swollen leg ten days after surgery
cases.opening: Sunita Patil, 52, is sitting on the ward bed with her left leg raised on a pillow. She had an operation ten days ago and for three days the leg has been aching and swelling. Introduce yourself and take a history.
cases.fallback: I am not sure what you mean. Can you ask that a different way?

patient.name: Sunita Patil
patient.occupation: Homemaker, looks after a joint family
patient.residence: Small town, lives with husband, two sons and mother-in-law

cues: why have you come to hospital
how can I help you today
presenting.reply: Doctor, my left leg has become swollen and painful since three days. I had my uterus operation ten days back, and now I am afraid something has gone wrong.

cues: was the onset gradual or sudden
onset_course.reply: It started three days ago, quite suddenly. The calf first felt tight in the evening, and by next morning the whole lower leg was swollen. It has only increased since.

cues: what kind of pain is it
is the calf tender to touch
calf_pain_ache.reply: It is a deep aching pain in the calf, like a constant cramp. Touching the calf hurts, and my son says the muscle feels hard compared to the other side.

cues: is the swelling on one side
how far up does the swelling go
swelling above the knee or below
leg_swelling_side.reply: Only the left leg. The swelling is from the foot up to just below the knee. The right leg is completely normal.

cues: effect of standing on the pain
walking_standing_effect.reply: Walking makes it much worse, the calf feels ready to burst. Lying down with the leg raised on a pillow gives some relief. I am limping now.

cues: is the leg warm or red
are the surface veins more visible
warmth_redness_look.reply: The leg feels warmer than the right one, and slightly red over the calf. The thin veins on the shin look more prominent than before.

fever_present.reply: I feel slightly feverish since yesterday, but there were no rigors or shivering fits.

breath_chest_warning.reply: No, my breathing is comfortable. There is no chest pain and I am not breathless even on walking to the bathroom.

cough_blood_warning.reply: No cough at all, and certainly no blood.

cues: how long were you in bed after surgery
surgery_recent_event.reply: I had my uterus removed ten days ago under general anaesthesia. I was in bed for almost a week and only started walking inside the house three days back, just when the leg pain began.

travel_bedrest_still.reply: No long journey. I have hardly left the house since the operation, mostly resting in bed.

cancer_weight_screen.reply: No cancer, and my weight and appetite were steady before this operation. The surgery was for fibroids, which the doctor said were not cancerous.

hormone_pill_use.reply: I took hormonal tablets for heavy bleeding for about a year before the operation, but stopped when surgery was fixed. Nothing since.

clot_before_history.reply: Nothing like this has ever happened to me before. I have never taken blood thinners.

varicose_vein_past.reply: I never had prominent veins or ulcers. My legs were always normal before this week.

tobacco_smoke_habit.reply: I have never smoked or chewed tobacco.

cues: any blood pressure or sugar medicines
drug_medicine_intake.reply: Only iron tablets after the operation, and paracetamol for pain. No sugar or pressure medicines, no steroids.

cues: anyone at home with lung clot
family_clot_history.reply: Nobody in our family has had leg clots or long-term blood thinner treatment. My mother had two miscarriages long ago, but nothing else.

other_illness_background.reply: No diabetes, no pressure, no heart trouble. Apart from the fibroid operation, I have never been admitted to hospital.

skill.gen.appearance.finding: Comfortable middle-aged woman, sitting with the left leg elevated. No breathlessness, no distress at rest.

skill.gen.vitals.finding: Temperature 37.8 C. Pulse 96 regular. Blood pressure 128/82. Respiratory rate 18. SpO2 98 percent on room air.

skill.gen.edema.finding: Left leg pitting oedema from foot to just below the knee. Calf 3 cm larger than the right at 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity. Right leg normal.

skill.exam.surg.varicose_inspection_palp.finding: Left calf warm, mildly red, tender and firm to feel along its whole length. Superficial veins on the shin dilated. No hard cord, no eczema, no ulcer. No varicose trunks on either side.

skill.exam.surg.arterial_pulses_lower.finding: Femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses present and equal on both sides. Foot warm with normal capillary refill.

skill.exam.surg.perthes_deep_vein_patenc.finding: Full walking tourniquet test deferred: forceful exercise against a possibly blocked deep system risks dislodging clot. No dorsiflexion or calf squeezing manoeuvre performed; calf tenderness and firmness noted on gentle palpation only, deep patency left to duplex.

duplex_leg.label: Compression duplex of the left leg
duplex_leg.result: Left popliteal and posterior tibial segments non-compressible with absent flow. Femoral vein patent with normal compressibility.
duplex_leg.note: This confirms a proximal thrombosis and is the proof the Wells likelihood pointed toward; a negative scan here would have sent the workup back to the start.

d_dimer_blood.label: Plasma d-dimer
d_dimer_blood.note: Supports the decision to scan in a high-likelihood patient, but it cannot confirm thrombosis on its own and would never have been enough to exclude it.

ascending_venogram.label: Ascending contrast venography
ascending_venogram.note: Historical test that once mapped clots before ultrasound; invasive and superseded by duplex, so not indicated when duplex is available.

ctpa_chest.label: CT pulmonary angiography
ctpa_chest.note: Not indicated: she has no breathlessness, chest pain, tachycardia or desaturation. Ordering it from reflex would add contrast and radiation without a question to answer.

differentialModel.answer: Acute proximal deep vein thrombosis of the left leg. Consider cellulitis, a ruptured Baker cyst, a calf muscle strain, superficial thrombophlebitis, lymphoedema, and pulmonary embolism as coexisting danger.

diagnosis.answer: Acute provoked proximal deep vein thrombosis of the left leg, high Wells likelihood, ten days after hysterectomy.

managementModel.answer: Therapeutic anticoagulation started promptly with the class suited to a postoperative patient, duplex confirmation already in hand, graduated compression and early mobilisation, planned three-month course for a provoked event, counselling on bleeding, and referral back if breathlessness or chest pain appears.

teachingPoints: The setting is the diagnosis: ten days after surgery under general anaesthesia with a week in bed, a new unilateral calf pain with swelling is thrombosis until duplex says otherwise.
Tempo separates it from chronic disease: three days of swelling points to clot, not the months of venous insufficiency or lymphoedema.
A comfortable patient with normal breathing still needs the chest questions; embolism is asked about, not waited for.
Pulses decide the emergency: present and equal pulses keep this venous, while a pale pulseless leg would have meant arterial ischaemia within hours.
The full walking tourniquet test is forbidden in suspected acute thrombosis, as are dorsiflexion and calf squeezing manoeuvres; the deferral is documented and duplex gives the answer.
A raised d-dimer in a high-likelihood patient only supports scanning; it neither confirms nor, had it been negative, excludes.
Provoked by surgery means a three-month course, with bleeding advice and a clear instruction to return with breathlessness or chest pain.
